blocks.text: 1. A/B Testing

blocks.alt: Users split into groups, some seeing model A and others seeing model B

blocks.text: Model Registry, the previous topic, covered a Staging stage where a candidate model undergoes validation before promotion, but that validation happens offline, checked against a held-out dataset. A/B Testing validates a candidate model against real, live production traffic instead, a different kind of evidence.

Offline validation checks whether a model is accurate; A/B Testing checks whether that accuracy actually improves real business outcomes once the model is serving live users. This makes A/B Testing a different, complementary form of evidence to gather before granting a candidate model a full promotion to Production.
2. Why Offline Validation Alone Is Not Always Enough

blocks.alt: Offline validation still leaves real user behavior unknown

blocks.text: A held-out test set, however carefully constructed, can still differ subtly from live, current traffic, since real users behave in ways historical data does not always fully capture, especially as time passes and genuine behavioral patterns shift.

A better accuracy metric also does not always translate directly into a better business outcome. A model with a higher measured click-through prediction accuracy, for instance, might not actually raise real revenue at all, if the improvement happens to concentrate on predictions that do not meaningfully affect user behavior in practice.
3. The Split Mechanism

blocks.alt: An incoming user gets a random assignment into group A or group B

blocks.text: Incoming live traffic gets randomly split into two groups. Group A, the control, gets served by the current Production model, the one already trusted and already running. Group B, the treatment, gets served instead by the candidate model being evaluated.

Each group's real, actual outcomes then get measured and compared directly against each other, giving a genuine, apples-to-apples comparison of how each model actually performs under identical, real-world conditions, rather than comparing two models against two potentially different offline datasets.

blocks.text: 4. Choosing What to Actually Measure

blocks.alt: An A/B test tracks a primary metric and guardrail metrics

blocks.text: A model-level metric, prediction accuracy for instance, is useful and easy to compute, but it is not always the real, final goal an organization actually cares about. A business-level metric, click-through rate, revenue, or user retention for instance, sits considerably closer to what matters to the organization running the test.

A well-designed A/B test typically tracks both: the model-level metric to understand the model's own technical performance, and the business-level metric to understand whether that technical performance actually translates into something the organization values.

blocks.text: 5. Statistical Significance

blocks.alt: An observed difference runs through a significance test to check if it is real or just chance

blocks.text: A raw, observed difference between Group A and Group B's measured outcomes could reflect a genuine effect, or it could simply be random noise, an artifact of which particular users happened to land in each group.

Statistical significance testing determines whether an observed difference is likely to be real, rather than merely chance variation. The practical rule is to never conclude a winner from a difference that is not actually statistically significant, regardless of how appealing that difference might look at first glance.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Declaring a winner based on an observed difference that has not actually cleared statistical significance is one of the most common, and most consequential, mistakes made when running A/B tests in practice.

blocks.text: 6. Sample Size and Duration

blocks.alt: Too small a sample produces an unreliable result

blocks.text: A trustworthy A/B test needs sufficient sample size, since too few users assigned to each group makes genuine noise indistinguishable from a real, meaningful effect, no matter how carefully the statistical test itself is applied afterward.

It also needs sufficient duration, since ending a test too early risks reacting to a temporary, unrepresentative fluctuation, a single unusual day of traffic for instance, rather than a stable, durable pattern that will actually hold once the model is fully deployed going forward.
7. Guardrail Metrics

A genuine risk in any A/B test is optimizing the primary metric while quietly harming something else entirely. Guardrail metrics are additional metrics tracked specifically to catch exactly this, a model raising click-through rate for instance while quietly increasing latency or error rate at the same time.

A test can only be called a success if the primary metric improves and every guardrail metric also stays healthy throughout, since a win on paper that comes bundled with a hidden, serious regression elsewhere is not actually a genuine win for the organization as a whole.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Choosing good guardrail metrics ahead of time, before a test even starts, is considerably better practice than only investigating for side effects after a surprising or concerning result already appears.

blocks.text: 8. The Decision Flow

blocks.alt: A test result leads to shipping the winner

blocks.text: An A/B test runs for its planned duration, determined by its sample size and duration requirements. At the end of that period, the question becomes whether the primary metric's improvement is statistically significant, and whether every guardrail metric has stayed healthy throughout the test.

If both conditions hold, the candidate gets promoted to full Production, flowing directly into the Model Registry promotion process. If either condition fails, the candidate does not get promoted, and the team instead investigates why the model did not translate into a genuine, real-world improvement.
9. When A/B Testing Matters Most

A/B Testing matters most for a high-stakes model change that directly affects real user experience or revenue, where offline metrics alone are simply not sufficient evidence for a decision carrying this much risk.

It also matters when comparing two different modeling approaches, not merely a minor retraining update, since live behavior can reveal real differences that offline evaluation, by its very nature, misses entirely.
10. Worked Example
The example below simulates a simple A/B test, comparing conversion rates between a control and treatment group and checking statistical significance.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)

group_a_size = 5000
group_b_size = 5000
group_a_conversions = rng.binomial(1, 0.10, size=group_a_size)  # current production model
group_b_conversions = rng.binomial(1, 0.115, size=group_b_size)  # candidate model

rate_a = group_a_conversions.mean()
rate_b = group_b_conversions.mean()

t_statistic, p_value = stats.ttest_ind(group_a_conversions, group_b_conversions)

print(f"Group A (control) conversion rate: {rate_a:.4f}")
print(f"Group B (treatment) conversion rate: {rate_b:.4f}")
print(f"Relative improvement: {(rate_b - rate_a) / rate_a:.2%}")
print(f"p-value: {p_value:.4f}")

if p_value < 0.05:
    print("Statistically significant improvement: candidate model can proceed toward promotion")
else:
    print("Not statistically significant: do not promote based on this result alone")

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A p-value below 0.05 is a common significance threshold, but it is a convention, not a universal law. Many production A/B testing frameworks use additional corrections when running multiple simultaneous tests, to avoid falsely declaring significance by chance.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: A/B Testing validates a candidate model against real, live production traffic, not just an offline held-out set.
A better offline accuracy metric does not always translate into a better real business outcome.
Live traffic splits randomly into a control group and a treatment group, compared directly on real outcomes.
A model-level metric like accuracy is useful, but a business-level metric is closer to what matters.
Statistical significance testing distinguishes a genuine effect from random noise; never conclude a winner without it.
A trustworthy test needs sufficient sample size and duration to avoid noise and temporary fluctuations.
Guardrail metrics catch a model that improves the primary metric while quietly harming something else.
Promotion to Production requires both statistical significance and healthy guardrails, flowing into the Model Registry.
